lessons.title: Unknown quantities: what changes, what stays
lessons.anchor: A garden had 95 flowers and now has 143. How many were planted?
lessons.diagnosis: A learner adds 95+143 because both numbers appear in the story.
lessons.concrete: Start with 95 counters. Add unknown counters until the collection reaches 143.
lessons.visual: Draw a tape bar of length 143 with a known segment 95 and an unknown segment.
lessons.self_check: 95+48=143. The change is smaller than the final total.
socratic: Which number describes the final amount?
Is the unknown the start, the change, or the end?
How can we undo adding an unknown amount?
lessons.remediation: If the student adds 95+143, label each quantity on the tape and ask whether the total can be smaller than that sum.
lessons.mastery: A shelf had 78 books and now has 121. How many were added?

lessons.title: Equal groups, inverse operations and remainder meaning
lessons.anchor: A group of 74 students travels in vans holding at most 8 students. What is the minimum number of vans?
lessons.diagnosis: A learner divides 74 by 8, truncates to 9 and forgets the two students left over.
lessons.concrete: Place 74 tokens into trays holding at most eight; fill nine trays and place the remaining two in another.
lessons.visual: Draw nine full boxes of 8 and one partial box of 2.
lessons.alternative: Check capacity: 9×8=72 is too small; 10×8=80 is sufficient.
lessons.self_check: All 74 students have seats; no van holds more than 8.
socratic: What does the quotient 9 remainder 2 mean in this story?
Can the two remaining students travel without a van?
What is the smallest whole number of vans with enough seats?
lessons.remediation: Ask the learner to model the two leftover students as tokens that must be seated.
lessons.mastery: A camp has 65 students and buses hold at most 12. What is the minimum number of buses?

lessons.title: Identify the whole before calculating a fraction
lessons.anchor: Twelve marbles are 3/7 of a collection. How many marbles are in the collection?
lessons.diagnosis: A learner computes 12×3/7 and treats the given part as the whole.
lessons.concrete: Build three equal groups of four counters to represent the known 12; extend to seven groups.
lessons.visual: Draw a seven-section bar. Shade three sections labeled 12 in total; each section is 4.
socratic: Does 12 describe the entire collection or only three sevenths?
How many marbles belong to one seventh?
How many sevenths make a whole?
lessons.remediation: Use seven equal boxes before writing an equation; the learner must label the three known boxes.
lessons.mastery: Fifteen beads are 3/8 of a set. How many beads are in the set?

lessons.title: Separate fixed fees from per-unit rates
lessons.anchor: A bike rental charges $9 to start and $4 per hour. What is the cost of 7 hours?
lessons.diagnosis: A learner calculates 9×7+4, mistakenly multiplying the fixed fee.
lessons.concrete: Show one $9 entry ticket and seven $4 hour tokens.
lessons.visual: Use a bar with one fixed $9 block followed by seven equal $4 blocks.
lessons.alternative: Make a table: 0 h→$9, 1 h→$13, 2 h→$17; continue adding $4 to 7 h.
lessons.self_check: Seven hours cost more than six by exactly $4, not $9.
socratic: Which amount is charged only once?
What changes with each extra hour?
Would doubling the hours double the entire bill?
lessons.remediation: Ask the learner to model a zero-hour bill; it should still be $9.
lessons.mastery: A rental has a $6 setup charge plus $5 per hour. What is the cost for 8 hours?

lessons.title: Area, perimeter and missing dimensions
lessons.anchor: A rectangle has perimeter 54 cm and width 11 cm. What is its length?
lessons.diagnosis: A learner subtracts 11 from 54, counting only one width.
lessons.concrete: Trace the four edges of a paper rectangle; mark opposite edges equal.
lessons.visual: Label two widths 11 and two unknown lengths x around the boundary.
lessons.alternative: Half the perimeter is length+width: 54÷2=27; length=27−11=16.
lessons.self_check: 2×(16+11)=54 cm. Perimeter uses cm, not cm².
socratic: How many sides does the perimeter include?
Why can we halve the perimeter first?
How can you verify the missing side?
lessons.remediation: Have the learner trace every edge and count both equal widths before calculating.
lessons.mastery: A rectangle has perimeter 68 cm and width 14 cm. What is its length?

lessons.title: Represent two ticket types with one variable
lessons.anchor: A theater sold 30 tickets: adults cost $12, children cost $8, total revenue $320. How many adults?
lessons.diagnosis: A learner assumes all 30 tickets have the same price.
lessons.concrete: Arrange 30 ticket cards, each initially priced at $8. Upgrading a card to adult adds $4.
lessons.visual: Show a baseline bar of 30×$8=$240 and an extra $80 made from $4 upgrades.
lessons.alternative: Start with all children: $240; remaining $80 at $4 extra per adult means 20 adults.
socratic: How many children are there if adults are a?
What revenue would all-child tickets produce?
How much extra revenue does one adult ticket create?
lessons.remediation: Use the upgrade-card model before asking the learner to write a two-term revenue equation.
lessons.mastery: A concert sells 25 tickets: adults $15, children $9, total $303. How many adult tickets?
